title: Kiln furniture and shelf placement
subtitle: How to stack shelves, use posts, and load a kiln for even heat distribution and maximum capacity
excerpt: Kiln furniture , shelves and posts , determines how pots are stacked and spaced in the kiln. Poor stacking means cold spots, glaze damage between pieces, and wasted space. This technique covers shelf and post selection, efficient multi-tier loading, how to identify and account for hot and cold zones in a standard electric top-loading kiln, and the rules for positioning glazed and unglazed ware together.
sourceNotes: Kiln furniture and shelf placement technique derived from first principles.

content.text: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Wear a P100 respirator when applying kiln wash to shelves (dry alumina and kaolin powder). Wet-clean only. Do not open a hot kiln below 80 degrees C. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach of the kiln area. Adequate ventilation when firing.

A well-loaded kiln fires more evenly, uses less energy per piece, and protects your work. Most studio potters stack inefficiently , too much space between pieces, underloaded shelves, or all tall pieces on the same tier. This technique covers the principles that apply to any top-loading electric kiln.
Kiln wash: the first step
Apply
kiln wash

to every shelf before the first use and after any glaze drip that has been scraped off. Mix kiln wash powder (equal parts alumina hydrate and calcined kaolin) with water to a thick cream. Paint two to three coats onto the top surface of each shelf. Allow to dry before firing. Never apply kiln wash to the bottom face of shelves.
Shelf and post selection

Use three posts per shelf for stability , not four. Three points always define a flat plane; a fourth post can cause the shelf to rock if the kiln floor is uneven. Posts must all be exactly the same height on a given tier. If posts are mismatched in height, the shelf tilts and pots slide.
Loading rules for glazed stoneware
Leave at least 15 mm between every glazed piece and any neighbouring piece or the kiln wall. Glazes flow at temperature; contact results in pieces fusing together or to the kiln wall.
Never stack glazed pieces directly on top of each other. Each tier of glazed ware needs its own shelf.

Plan shelf height for each tier based on your tallest piece on that shelf, plus post height plus 20 mm minimum clearance above the lid of the tallest piece. Standard post increments: 25 mm, 50 mm, 75 mm, 100 mm. Combine posts to reach the needed height. Example: a 90 mm pot needs a 100 mm post to sit clear of the shelf above. A 150 mm pot needs 175 mm clearance , use a 100 mm plus a 75 mm post stacked.

Place the tallest pieces in the hottest zone of the kiln , in a standard top-loading electric kiln, this is the middle third. The top of the kiln is slightly cooler due to heat loss through the lid; the very bottom is cooler due to the insulating kiln floor mass.
The
cold spot
at the top of the kiln is usable for
bisque
ware placed on the top shelf, or for glaze-firing pieces that tolerate a slightly lower
cone
. Do not fire critical glazed pieces on the top shelf.
How to stack bisqueware efficiently

Bisque ware does not have liquid glaze, so pieces can touch or stack inside each other (bowls nesting rim-to-rim, cups stacked inside each other). Pack bisque loads tight. One bisque load can hold three to four times as many pieces as a glaze load of the same size. Use bisque loads to test new forms and clay bodies before committing to glaze firing costs.

rows.problem: Two pieces fused together after firing
rows.cause: Pieces were placed too close together and glaze flowed across the gap
rows.fix: Check glaze edges before loading: any glaze drip pointing toward another piece is a risk. Maintain 15-20 mm minimum clearance. If pieces fused, chisel them apart carefully and grind the fused spot with a diamond grinding pad.

rows.problem: Pot fused to kiln shelf , glaze on base
rows.cause: Glaze on the foot-ring or base was not removed before loading
rows.fix: Before loading, always run a finger along every foot-ring to feel for glaze grit. Scrape and grind any glazed shelf surfaces to kiln wash, and re-coat with kiln wash before the next firing.

rows.cause: Shelf loaded unevenly, placing the unsupported middle under thermal stress; or an old shelf with existing small cracks
rows.fix: Check all shelves for hairline cracks before each firing. Use three evenly-spaced posts and centre the heaviest pieces directly over the post positions.
